Quantum Universe
Photo: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage Team
Answering the unresolved questions about the universe
At Quantum Universe, the focus is on the Higgs particle and its significance for the development of the universe from its origins to the present day. We are a leader in the technology development for gravitational wave detectors and our cluster benefits from synergies between experiments on dark matter and gravitational waves. The combination of new ideas from theoretical physics with modern mathematical structures enables significant advances in the description of quantum gravity. And we develop innovative methods of artificial intelligence that enable efficient and resource-saving processing of large amounts of research data.
Photo: Xiaoze Tan
Join the Quantum Universe team
During the startup phase of our second funding period, we are opening more than 50 doctoral and postdoctoral positions in our Cluster of Excellence. Are you an outstanding Master's student, doctoral or postdoctoral researcher with excellent degrees and scientific track record in one of the Cluster's research areas, i.e. Higgs physics, Dark Matter and Axions, Gravitational Waves, Quantum Gravity, Algebraic and Geometric Structures, Artificial Intelligence, as well as Detectors, Quantum Sensors and Accelerators?
Apply to one of our positions and become part of the Quantum Universe team!
Who we are
Quantum Universe in 90 seconds
At the University of Hamburg's Cluster of Excellence “Quantum Universe”, we are investigating the greatest unsolved mysteries of the universe. Our goal is to better understand the relationship between mass and gravity. To this end, we work closely with our cooperation partner DESY and research institutions worldwide.

Experts in Quantum Gravity Meet in Hamburg for DESY Theory Workshop
For almost 40 years, theoretical physicists from around the world have met at DESY for the annual DESY Theory Workshop. Last week, 160 leading scientists and early-career researchers came together to discuss their work and exchange ideas at the Science City Campus Bahrenfeld in Hamburg.

How Long Does a Higgs Boson Live?
New analysis involving Quantum Universe researchers determines the Higgs boson’s lifetime to about 10% precision — something the Large Hadron Collider cannot measure directly.

Where Algebra Meets Strings: The CRC 1624 Summer School
Three weeks, 17 speakers from around the world, and over 120 participants gathered in Hamburg for an intensive program at the frontier of mathematics and theoretical physics.

In Search of Unknown Forces
The CMS experiment at CERN, with key contributions from the Cluster of Excellence Quantum Universe at the University of Hamburg, sets the world's most precise limits yet on how force-carrying particles interact — narrowing down where new, undiscovered physics could be hiding.
